summary: The hajj is the pilgrimage to Mecca, counted in Sunni and Shiʿi tradition among the pillars of Islam and held to be obligatory once in a lifetime on every adult Muslim who is able to undertake it. The Qur'an makes pilgrimage to the House a duty on those able (Q 3:97) and commands its completion for God (Q 2:196), and the tradition performs it through a set of rites in and around Mecca during the appointed days. It is also a gathering of the worldwide Muslim community (umma), whose members enter a common state and dress of consecration (ihram).
description:
The hajj is the annual pilgrimage to Mecca and its surrounding sacred sites, performed during the month of Dhu al-Hijja. In the standard tradition it is one of the pillars of Islam, an obligation (fard) upon every Muslim who is adult, sane, and able (in body and means) to make the journey, to be performed at least once in a lifetime. Its Qur'anic basis is direct: Q 3:97, in the Sahih International rendering, states, 'And [due] to Allah from the people is a pilgrimage to the House, for whoever is able to find thereto a way'; Q 2:196 commands, 'And complete the hajj and ʿumra for Allah'; and Q 2:197 begins, 'Hajj is [during] well-known months,' setting the pilgrimage within appointed times and enjoining restraint from quarrelling and wrongdoing during it. Q 22:27 has God command that the pilgrimage be proclaimed to the people, 'they will come to you on foot and on every lean camel, they will come from every distant pass.' The distinction between the greater pilgrimage (hajj), tied to the appointed days, and the lesser pilgrimage (ʿumra), which may be performed at other times, is drawn in the sources.

The tradition also grounds the pillar in the Sunna. A widely transmitted hadith, reported in the canonical collections on the authority of Ibn ʿUmar, states that Islam is built upon five, and includes the pilgrimage to the House among them, alongside the testimony of faith, the prayer, the alms, and the fast of Ramadan; this report is cited here as the tradition's own attestation of hajj as a pillar.

The rites are described here as the tradition's attributed practice. The pilgrim first enters ihram, the consecrated state, putting on (for men) two seamless white cloths and abstaining from certain ordinary acts, and pronouncing the talbiya. The central rites include the tawaf, the sevenfold circumambulation of the Kaʿba, the cubic structure at the heart of the Sacred Mosque; the saʿy, the going seven times between the hills of Safa and Marwa; and, as the essential standing of the hajj, the wuquf at ʿArafat on the ninth of Dhu al-Hijja. Further rites include the stay at Muzdalifa, the stoning of pillars at Mina, and the sacrifice, after which the pilgrim leaves the state of ihram. Accounts of the sequence and details differ across the legal schools and are given here in brief and in outline, not as a ruling on any school's practice.

The hajj carries a strong social dimension in the tradition's own account. It gathers Muslims from across the world in one place and time, and the common dress of ihram is widely read as levelling distinctions of rank and wealth before God, so that the pilgrimage is presented as an enactment of the unity and equality of the community (umma). This entry describes the hajj on the tradition's own terms and reports its rites and their meanings as that tradition's account, without adjudicating them.

relations.note: The hajj is counted among the pillars of Islam, the acts the tradition treats as the framework of Muslim practice; described here on the tradition's own terms.

The ʿumra (lesser pilgrimage) is distinguished from the hajj (greater pilgrimage): the ʿumra may be performed at other times, while the hajj is tied to the appointed days, and Q 2:196 commands the completion of both for God. Target is a forward reference; umra does not yet exist as an entry.

Shared question: both the hajj and the Jewish aliyah la-regel are a tradition's pilgrimage to a central sacred place that gathers the community. Difference: the hajj is an obligatory pillar performed at Mecca once in a lifetime by those able, whereas the aliyah la-regel was the ascent to the Temple in Jerusalem on the three pilgrimage festivals (regalim); no ranking or equivalence is asserted (neutrality #10). Target (aliyah-la-regel) exists in the dataset.

Shared question: both the hajj and Christian pilgrimage are sacred journeys to holy places undertaken as an act of devotion and communal gathering. Difference: the hajj is an obligatory pillar with fixed rites and times, whereas Christian pilgrimage (to Jerusalem, Rome, Santiago, and other sites) is a non-obligatory devotional practice; the shared theme is stated without ranking either (neutrality #10). Target (christian-pilgrimage) exists in the dataset.

historical_period.note: The Qur'anic verses grounding the hajj (Q 3:97, 2:196-197, 22:27) belong to the period of the Prophet's mission (c. 610-632 CE); the tradition holds the pilgrimage to reach back to Abraham (Ibrahim) and traces the standard rites to the Prophet's Farewell Pilgrimage. The pilgrimage remains a living annual practice; no end date is asserted.
